platform-engineering-fundamentals.description: The vocabulary every platform interview opens with: what a platform actually is, why self-service is the defining property, and where platform engineering sits against DevOps and SRE.
study_notes: Can you define a platform without listing tools?
The precise boundary between platform engineering, DevOps, and SRE.
When an organisation should not build a platform at all.

developer-experience.description: The user side of the platform: cognitive load, service catalogues, portals, scorecards, onboarding time, and the metrics that tell you whether developers are actually better off.
study_notes: How you measure developer experience without counting story points.
Why cognitive load, not tool count, is the design constraint.
What a scorecard must avoid to survive contact with real teams.

platform-architecture.description: Designing the platform itself: control plane versus data plane, the developer-facing API, escapable abstractions, interface versioning, and build-versus-buy.
study_notes: The developer-facing contract, and what belongs in it versus behind it.
How you version a platform interface and migrate consumers for them.
Why leak-proof abstractions turn the platform team into a bottleneck.

multi-tenancy-and-isolation.description: Sharing infrastructure without sharing blast radius: tenancy models, namespace versus cluster boundaries, noisy neighbours, quotas, network isolation, and per-tenant accounting.
study_notes: Which isolation boundary a given threat model actually requires.
Why a Kubernetes namespace is a soft boundary, and what hardens it.
How you offboard a tenant completely, including its data and cost trail.

kubernetes-platform.description: Kubernetes as the substrate: cluster topology, node pools and scheduling, fleet upgrades, admission control as a platform lever, operators, and service mesh.
study_notes: Cluster-per-what - the topology decision and its cost.
How you upgrade a fleet without breaking tenant workloads.
When a controller or operator is the right answer, and when it is not.

control-planes-and-abstractions.description: Turning infrastructure into a self-service API: Crossplane, custom resources as platform contracts, workload specifications, Terraform at scale, and safe resource lifecycle.
study_notes: Control-plane reconciliation versus run-to-completion IaC.
How you expose infrastructure without handing out cloud credentials.
What protects a stateful resource from an accidental delete.

gitops-and-continuous-delivery.description: Git as the source of truth: Argo CD and Flux, repository structure at scale, environment promotion, secrets, drift detection, and self-service pipelines that do not multiply.
study_notes: What GitOps actually guarantees, and what it does not.
How a change is promoted between environments without copy-paste.
Where secrets live when the desired state is in a public-ish repo.

progressive-delivery-and-feature-flags.description: Separating deploy from release: flags as a platform capability, flag debt and its SLAs, rollout curves with abort criteria, trustworthy kill switches, and consistent bucketing.
study_notes: Deploy versus release, and which risk each one controls.
The abort threshold and hold time for every rollout phase, set before it starts.
What a flag flip cannot undo - state, not behaviour.

environments-and-ephemeral-infrastructur.description: Environments on demand: preview environments per pull request, data seeding without leaking production, environment parity, cost control, and the inner development loop.
study_notes: What a preview environment must include to be trusted.
How you seed realistic data without copying real customer records.
Which dimensions of environment parity actually matter.

platform-security.description: Security as a platform default: workload identity without long-lived keys, secretless pipelines, secrets management, supply-chain provenance, base image currency, and break-glass access.
study_notes: How a workload proves who it is without a stored credential.
The supply-chain chain of custody from commit to running container.
How you patch every service at once when a critical CVE lands.

policy-as-code-and-governance.description: Guardrails that are code: OPA and Kyverno, rolling out policy without breaking teams, compliance frameworks mapped to enforceable controls, exception handling, and audit trails.
study_notes: Guardrail versus gate, and where each belongs in the flow.
How you introduce a policy that would currently fail production.
Turning a SOC 2 or PCI control into something a machine checks.

aws-platform-engineering.description: Building a platform on AWS: multi-account organisation design, account vending, EKS pod identity, runtime selection, Karpenter capacity, paved-road self-service, and cost allocation.
study_notes: Why the account is the primary isolation boundary on AWS.
How a pod gets AWS permissions without an access key.
The runtime decision between ECS, EKS, Lambda, and App Runner.

azure-platform-engineering.description: Building a platform on Azure: management groups and landing zones, Azure Policy guardrails, AKS workload identity, runtime selection, Bicep modules, and private networking for PaaS.
study_notes: The management group / subscription / resource group hierarchy and what each buys.
Azure Policy as the enforcement point rather than a reporting tool.
When Container Apps beats AKS, and why that is usually the right default.

gcp-platform-engineering.description: Building a platform on GCP: the folder and project hierarchy, organisation policies, Workload Identity Federation, GKE versus Cloud Run, Shared VPC, and Config Connector.
study_notes: Why the project is the unit of isolation and billing on GCP.
How Workload Identity Federation eliminates service account keys.
Shared VPC and the host/service project split.

multi-cloud-and-hybrid-platforms.description: When more than one cloud is real: genuine drivers versus slogans, the cost of portable abstractions, cross-provider primitive mapping, hybrid designs, and data gravity.
study_notes: The business or compliance driver that justifies a second cloud.
What you give up by abstracting over managed services.
Why egress and data gravity decide most of these arguments.

platform-reliability.description: Keeping the platform up: SLOs for a platform rather than an app, error budget policy, platform on-call, incidents where the platform is the incident, graceful degradation, and DR.
study_notes: What you can promise when your users are other engineers.
How the platform keeps serving traffic while its control plane is down.
Recovering the platform when the tooling you would use is also gone.

platform-observability.description: Telemetry as a platform capability: OpenTelemetry collectors as shared infrastructure, cardinality and cost control, zero-effort instrumentation, cross-tenant tracing, and adoption signals.
study_notes: What a service should get for free, with no instrumentation work.
Where observability cost comes from, and which lever actually cuts it.
Measuring platform usage from the telemetry you already collect.

platform-finops.description: The money side of the platform: cost attribution for shared infrastructure, showback versus chargeback, unit economics, commitment and spot strategy, and idle spend.
study_notes: How you attribute a shared control plane or NAT gateway fairly.
Why showback usually changes behaviour and chargeback often does not.
Cost per unit of business value, not cost per month.

platform-team-and-operating-model.description: Running the team: Team Topologies, staffing, adoption metrics, migration without a mandate, deprecation, the RFC process, and a roadmap that can say no.
study_notes: Platform team as an enabling team, not a ticket queue.
Adoption as the success metric, and what it must be adjusted for.
How you deprecate something teams still depend on.

platform-engineering-interviews.description: How the interview itself works: the loop structure, the platform design round, presenting your own platform work, troubleshooting rounds, behavioural themes, and what to ask back.
study_notes: The platform design round is about the interface and the users, not the diagram.
How to tell a platform story with an outcome rather than a tool list.
The questions that reveal whether their platform is real.
